answer: A piece of advice I would give to any young person is not to be afraid of failure, but to see it as part of learning. It sounds like a cliché, but I think very few people actually live by it. I think this is genuinely important because so many young people are [[paralysed]] by the fear of getting things wrong. In my country especially, exam results are treated as a matter of family honour, so failing can feel like a disaster rather than a lesson. I would give this advice to my younger cousins, who sometimes hesitate to try new things in case they fail. I would also share it with the students I meet at work, many of whom are too scared to apply to good universities in case they are rejected. I would tell them that every successful person has failed countless times, and that setbacks are often the most [[instructive]] experiences of all. The key is to be [[resilient]] and to keep going. A rejection letter or a poor mark is simply information about what to improve next time, not a judgement on who you are. I believe this mindset could help them enormously, freeing them to take risks and pursue their dreams. Honestly, I wish someone had drilled this into me when I was younger, because I wasted opportunities out of fear. I think teaching young people to embrace failure rather than dread it is one of the most [[invaluable]] lessons we can offer them. It builds courage and confidence for life, and it makes the journey far less [[nerve-racking]].

followUps.q: Who gave you the best advice when you were younger?
followUps.answer: Probably my grandmother. She had little formal education, but she used to say that a tree that bends in the storm doesn't break. It took me years to appreciate how [[profound]] that was.

followUps.q: Do young people usually listen to advice?
followUps.answer: Not always, especially if it sounds like a lecture. I think they listen more when advice comes with a personal story, so they can see that you have actually been through it yourself.

note: Added cultural pressure around exams and students at his consultancy as a second audience; plain 'valuable' became [[invaluable]], added [[nerve-racking]].
